lines.text: doctrine agree with the teaching of our parable which
implies that God is the master whose slaves we are? Are we
here still moving within the atmosphere of the gospel of good
news?
It would be an obvious answer to say that we should not
isolate this parable and view it as a detached saying. We
must complete it. We must take it together with the other
sayings of Jesus which speak of God as loving Father, with
the words of grace and mercy. Of course we must do so.
But the composite view must not be so constructed that we
complete one feature by adding another, and so make for
ourselves a selective picture of Jesus and His message in
which one feature tones down another, in which the greatness
and the power of the one is weakened by the other, so that
finally there issues a picture of Jesus which is muddled and
diluted; a picture which at bottom is shaped according to
our own tastes and wishes. No; the composite whole must
emerge in a different manner. It must arise from a process in
which one saying explains another, in which we understand
one word in the light of another, so that in the end every
word of Jesus is seen to disclose the one and the same Lord,
whose word is at one and the same time both terrifying and
consoling, a dismaying and a glad message. Only then have
we understood it fully.
What does this mean as far as our parable is concerned?
It means this, that we must not set alongside His teaching
here another message concerning the goodness and the grace
of God, but that we must understand this very parable as a
word of grace.
II
But how are we to understand this paradox, namely that
God precisely in so far as He is the Lord who deals with us
arbitrarily as His slaves, is at the same time the Father whose
loving-kindness governs us His children? How understand
that just that insight which we cannot fail to express: "We
are unworthy servants", is for us liberating, redeeming, saving?
We must at once remove a possible misunderstanding.
